transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-02-14
Start: 15:00 PST
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Samira Patel (Redwood AE), Ethan Moore (Redwood SE), Jordan Lee (Acme MLOps), Priya Kaur (Acme CTO), Michael Chen (Acme SRE)
Recording ID: ff-20250214-8347

Summary:
Redwood AE/SE walked Acme Health through an edge-case focused demo of Redwood API, Console, and Optimize. Topics: long context handling (large clinical notes), high TPS patterns and autoscaling, streaming backpressure and client signals, timeout & retry policies, graceful fallback to model variants, and Dedicated pool benchmark plan. Agreed next steps include sharing pricing/security docs and provisioning a short benchmark on Dedicated.

Topics covered:
- Long context / large documents (prefix caching, K-V cache behavior)
- High TPS load and batching/autoscaling
- Streaming backpressure, chunking, and client-side timeouts
- Timeouts, retry/backoff, and graceful degradation (model variant fallbacks)
- Console demos: route metrics, token-level breakdown, Optimize recommendations

Transcript (periodic timestamps, imperfect transcription):
[00:00] Samira: hey everyone, thanks for joining, i'll hand off to ethan for the technical walkthrough but quick intro, i'm samira, i'm the ae on the account.
[00:22] Ethan: hi jordan, priya, mike, thanks for your time. we're gonna focus on edge cases you called out — long clinical context, really high TPS loads, and what happens when streaming backpressure and timeouts kick in. bear with me if i jump between console and live API.
[00:45] Jordan: quick note, our primary concern is preserving context for long patient histories — we've got transcript files that are 40k to 100k tokens after encoding, so curious about the "long window" story. also, we need predictable latency at peak times, that's the big blocker for deployment.
[01:12] Ethan: yes, good. on long context we have two levers: first is model selection — some variants support much larger context windows, and second is our prefix/KV cache mechanism — we can cache encoded prefixes at the service layer so repeated reads don't re-encode. that reduces token compute. one caveat, if you have many unique prefixes caching hit rate drops.
[01:40] Priya: when you say "KV cache", is that per-route? per-tenant? how does it behave on Dedicated?
[01:52] Ethan: good question. by default it's per-route in hosted. on Dedicated you can configure per-tenant local KV caches pinned to the GPU pool — it avoids cross-tenant evictions. also we do TTL and LRU policies. i'll show the console.
[02:10] [Screen share; console opens] Ethan: here is the route metrics — you can see token breakdown, prefix cache hit rate, and latency percentiles. this demo run is synthetic — ignore absolute numbers, focus on the behavior lines.
[02:35] Michael: i see a spike at p95 after a context refresh. is that because of cache warmup?
[02:42] Ethan: exactly. first request after an uncached prefix will pay encode and KV fill cost. our recommended pattern is a warmup pass during onboarding or pre-warming high-frequency keys.
[03:05] Samira: also note Optimize will recommend batching and quantization settings based on your observed traffic — we'll demo that.
[03:22] Ethan: moving to high TPS. Acme said they expect bursts up to ~1k TPS for short windows. in hosting, we rely on continuous batching and a shard-based autoscaler. the key point: latency SLO vs cost tradeoff. we can keep latency low by overprovisioning Dedicated pool or accept slightly higher p99 and save cost via batching.
[03:52] Jordan: that 1k TPS is across many short calls, small prompt sizes, but high frequency. do you support per-route throttles? priority queues?
[04:05] Ethan: yes, we support per-route QoS, token quotas, and route-based priority. you can pin critical routes to a low-latency pool with reserved capacity. fallback policy will route lower priority traffic to cheaper model variants or queued batch windows.
[04:30] [00:04:30] Ethan: demoing streaming backpressure now — when clients can't read fast enough we send TCP-level signals and chunked encoding uses backpressure; Redwood will apply internal request queuing limits and expose backpressure signals in the SDK. if a stream is slow, the runtime can either buffer a bit, break the response into smaller chunks, or trigger a graceful abort depending on route policy.
[04:58] Priya: how do you surface that to app devs? we use a node streaming consumer, we need clear events for slow consumers.
[05:12] Ethan: our SDK emits events: onPart, onBackpressure, onAbort, and we document recommended client-side window sizes. on heavy backpressure we can also compress chunks and reduce precision if you enable quantization-fallback. note: sometimes the transcription shows relayed like 'on backpress' in logs — it's a little messy.
[05:40] Jordan: i saw a mention in your docs about "graceful degradation" — can you give a concrete flow?
[05:50] Ethan: sure. 1) if p50/p90 latency creeps, route policy can switch to a smaller model variant automatically (same API shape). 2) we can shorten response length heuristics (trim boilerplate) via prompt templates or safety tokens. 3) if streaming stalls, we finish with a truncated completion and set a flag so the app knows it was partial. these are configurable per-route.
[06:22] Michael: what about timeouts and retries — network retries vs model timeouts, and how you avoid double charging?
[06:32] Ethan: we support idempotency keys for requests to prevent double execution. model-side timeouts are applied server-side; if client times out and retries, idempotency key avoids re-run. for streaming, we recommend short client read timeouts and a finalization step to check if the response completed. SDKs handle this pattern.
[06:58] [07:15] Samira: quick interlude — on security: we have SOC 2 docs, SAML/SSO, and KMS integrations for key management — we'll share the whitepaper after this call.
[07:30] Priya: yes please. and do you support HSM? we have strict key custody rules.
[07:36] Ethan: yes, HSM via customer-managed KMS for Private deployments and Dedicated can be configured behind your KMS/HSM.
[07:50] Jordan: back to performance — can we run a short benchmark? we'd like to see real p50/p95 numbers on our prompts and real long contexts.
[08:02] Ethan: absolutely — typical POC flow: we provision a trial Dedicated pool for a week, you run your prompts and traffic generator, we capture metrics in the console and Optimize will produce batching/quantization recs.
[08:18] [09:00] Ethan: demoing the Optimize tab: here it pulls sample traffic and suggests batch sizes, quantization level (8-bit agnostic), and whether to enable prefix caching. for your workload with long docs, Optimize suggests: keep a local KV cache with 24h TTL and smaller batch windows for long-context reads to avoid memory pressure.
[09:40] Jordan: smaller batch windows reduces efficiency though, right? won't cost go up?
[09:47] Ethan: yes tradeoff. Optimize shows estimated cost delta — you can pick higher cost for lower latency. we also show a mixed policy: route critical calls with small batch/low latency, route analytic batch jobs to larger windows.
[10:10] Michael: curious about backpressure magnitudes. if a client is slow and we have 1k TPS incoming, do you start shedding? queueing? how do you protect the control plane?
[10:24] Ethan: we have a multi-tier approach: short-term in-memory queues, then token-aware shedding if queues exceed thresholds (we evict low-priority requests), then autoscaler kicks in. the console will surface queue length and 'shed' events. control plane is isolated for Dedicated so tenant issues don't affect global control plane.
[10:50] [12:05] Priya: what are the default timeout values and where do we tune them?
[12:12] Ethan: defaults: 60s model timeout, 30s client read timeout in SDK, but fully tunable per-route. for streaming we recommend client read < model timeout so you can retry safely.
[12:35] Jordan: any gotchas with idempotency and streaming?
[12:40] Ethan: streaming plus idempotency is tricky; our SDK writes a finalization record when stream completes — if client disconnects before that, it can retry with same key, and runtime will either resume (if KV cached) or start again but avoid double billing when possible. there's some edge behavior if you have partial stateful operations; we flagged that in docs.
[13:15] Samira: (aside) one note — sometimes our internal transcripts show product names slightly off, like 'Redwood Opti' or 'K-V cash' spelled wrong, that's just auto-transcribe artifacts.
[13:30] Ethan: walking through a simulated incident scenario: we pump 1k TPS for 2 minutes and throttle one route at random. watch the console: you can see p50 stays low for the pinned route, other routes degrade, Optimize suggests moving some traffic or adding reserved burst capacity.
[14:05] [19:20] Ethan: launching a live load test now — we're using a synthetic traffic generator with your sample prompts (submitted earlier). streaming responses are chunked every ~200 tokens in this test.
[19:38] Jordan: little background noise — is the load from many short prompts or long contexts?
[19:45] Ethan: mostly short prompts at high TPS for this particular test. separately we ran a long-context test with single requests that were 50k tokens; those show different memory behavior.
[21:02] Michael: in the long-context run did you observe GPU mem spikes? what quantization/attention changes helped?
[21:15] Ethan: yes, memory grows with context. two options: model variants with attention kernel optimizations (we pick those automatically) and offloading KV cache to local memory rather than GPU for cold items. Optimize recommended 8-bit quantization for longer contexts to fit in memory with minimal quality degradation.
[22:05] Priya: are there any hidden costs with caching large prefixes? network egress or storage cost?
[22:12] Ethan: cache storage is accounted in Dedicated pricing if you're on-prem/Private. hosted includes that in token costs but very large caches may push you to a Reserved commit. we'll detail in pricing.
[23:00] [30:00] Ethan: touching on timeouts again — in our tests we saw that with a 60s server timeout, streaming kept sending pieces until ~58s, and then finalization failed on client disconnects; recommended pattern is to implement incremental checkpointing in your app, and our SDK supports resume from a prefix id in some cases.
[30:40] Jordan: explain resume — is that reconstructing the prompt or resuming model state?
[30:48] Ethan: it's resume from prefix cache: if the prefix is cached and you provide the same id, we avoid re-encoding. we can't resume an in-progress KV cache that was ephemeral across a different model run, but for many use-cases reusing cached prefixes is sufficient.
[31:20] Priya: any regulatory constraints we should be aware of for healthcare? audit logs? data residency?
[31:30] Ethan: yes, Private deployments cover data residency; audit logs are available for all tiers but retention differs. we have HIPAA considerations for BAA — we can provide our legal/security pack for review.
[32:05] Samira: ok we're running low on time, last demo piece: console shows an automatic Optimize rec that suggested batching 8 -> 4 for long-context reads, and enabling a model-variant fallback.
[32:25] Ethan: that cut p95 by ~35% in our bench but raised token-cost per successful completion — tradeoff you can tune.
[33:10] Jordan: what's your recommendation for our initial POC?
[33:18] Ethan: provision a Dedicated small pool (2-4 GPUs) for a week, run both short-high-TPS and long-context scenarios, use Optimize to produce config. we'll help interpret results and propose commit sizing.
[33:40] Michael: timeline to spin that up?
[33:45] Samira: we can provision test Dedicated in 48 hours after you sign the trial SOW; i'll send the SOW and pilot pricing.
[34:00] [40:00] Priya: anything we should watch for in our instrumentation to get good Optimize recommendations?
[40:10] Ethan: yes, send your real prompt shapes, token distribution, and desired latency SLO. don't redact prompts too aggressively — Optimize needs representative text. also include client read speeds for streaming so we can tune chunk sizes.
[40:45] Jordan: ok i'll collate that and send it over.
[41:00] Ethan: final recap: we'll share SOC 2/HSM docs, Samira will send pricing and SOW, Ethan will provision benchmark infra notes and run initial load tests once we have sample prompts, Acme will share throughput numbers and sample prompts.
[41:25] Samira: and we'll set up a POC scoping meeting week of 2025-02-24.
[41:35] Priya: perfect. one small ask — competitors: we've been evaluating services from OpenAI and Anthropic — can you outline where Redwood's routing/fallback features differ?
[41:50] Samira: brief: Redwood focuses on unified serving across hosted/dedicated/private, built-in route-level fallback policies, and Optimize tooling that ties perf recommendations to cost. we'll send a short comparison doc.
[42:10] Jordan: thanks.
[42:20] Michael: thanks all.
[42:30] Samira: thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the docs and pricing.
[52:00] End recording.
